as_told: When Christopher Columbus proposed to sail west to reach Asia, the learned men of his time believed the earth was flat. They warned that his ships would sail off the edge of the world. Columbus, who knew the earth was round, proved them wrong in 1492.
lesson: The experts of Columbus's time were ignorant men who thought the earth was flat, and a bold visionary proved them wrong.
what_happened: Columbus's son Ferdinand wrote the earliest detailed account of the royal commission that judged Columbus's plan. The objections he records assume a round earth: that the world was too large to cross in three years, that only a small part of 'this lower globe of earth and water' was inhabited, and that a ship sailing down the curve of the globe could not climb back. No objection in his account says the earth is flat or that ships would fall off an edge. Washington Irving's 1828 biography turned the commission into a scene of churchmen quoting scripture, and wrote that some of them inferred from the Bible that the heavens and earth 'must be flat'; even Irving said that others 'admitted the globular form of the earth'. Popular medieval books such as Mandeville's Travels already taught that one could sail around the round earth.
false_part: Columbus's learned contemporaries did not believe the earth was flat or fear that he would sail off its edge; their objections were about the size of the globe, the length of the voyage and whether ships could return.

earliest_telling.where: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus, vol. 1 (London: John Murray), book II, chapter IV, 'Columbus before the Council at Salamanca', p. 124

lesson_verdict.why: The roundness of the earth was taught to ordinary readers long before 1492: a popular 14th-century travel book told them that a man could sail around the whole earth and come home. The doubts that Ferdinand Columbus records from the experts concerned distance and return, not shape.

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "Columbus" "earth was flat": 8,063 hits; the earliest dated hits were Kipling (1897, 1917) and a 1917 school history. Nothing before Irving's 1828 book was found.

Archive.org search: saved the djvu text of Irving, A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus, vol. 1 (London, 1828; historyoflifevoy01irvi). Pages 120-125 describe the council at Salamanca, with objections from Lactantius, St Augustine and the Psalms.
Irving's footnote cites Remesal, Historia de Chiapa (1619), book II, chapter 7, for the council. I did not find or read Remesal.

Archive.org search for an English text of Ferdinand Columbus: the Benjamin Keen translation (1959) is borrow-only; the 1744 Churchill volume II (b30455042_0002) turned out to hold other voyages; saved the 1732 Churchill volume II (cihm_33298), which contains Ferdinand's history, chapter XI.
Las Casas, Historia de las Indias: not searched.
No record was found of anyone at the time saying that Columbus would sail off the edge of the earth.
Lesson source: gutenberg.org was down for maintenance (503); saved the same eBook 782 from the Brown University mirror (atlas.cs.brown.edu).

HathiTrust and Google Books full-text search: HathiTrust refused with a Cloudflare check; Google Books API refused with 429; did not retry. Chronicling America (loc.gov) refused with 403; did not retry.
confidence_note: Ferdinand's account is in a 1704 English translation of a 1571 Italian translation of a lost Spanish text, so the wording is not Ferdinand's own; but the sense of the objections is clear. I did not check whether some telling of a flat-earth fear before Irving exists. The 'sail off the edge' detail has no source that I found.
